Understood: you want to know how the NetBird "agent-network" feature (docs.netbird.io/agent-network) integrates with the LiteLLM AI gateway. Specifically: whether NetBird groups are created in LiteLLM, how budgets are handled per team, and whether you are limited to teams that exist in the identity provider.## Short answer

- **NetBird does not create groups, teams or budgets in LiteLLM.** It adds the caller's group names to each request. LiteLLM sees them as tags.
- **Budgets exist in two independent layers.** NetBird enforces per-user and per-group budgets in its own policies. LiteLLM enforces tag budgets and end-user budgets, but only if you create them in LiteLLM.
- **You are not strictly limited to IdP teams.** Policies work on NetBird groups, and IdP sync is only one way to populate them. Groups that are not synced from the IdP are less clearly documented (see below).

## 1. Integration mechanism

The integration has three parts, all described on the [LiteLLM integration page](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm).

- **Provider setup.** You register your self-hosted LiteLLM as a provider and paste a LiteLLM virtual key. NetBird stores that key server-side. Agents call the NetBird endpoint with no key.
- **Identity forwarding.** The proxy forwards identity on each request:
  - "**Groups** are written into `metadata.tags` in the JSON body, so LiteLLM can apply tag budgets and rate limits."
  - "The **user identity** is sent in the `x-litellm-end-user-id` header."
  - The proxy strips any client-supplied values first, so callers can't spoof their identity. You can switch forwarding off per provider ("Forward identity metadata").
- **Virtual key requirement.** The virtual key must have `metadata.allow_client_tags: true`. Otherwise "LiteLLM silently drops the forwarded tags."

## 2. Are groups "created" in LiteLLM?

Not in the sense of provisioning. The docs say "each NetBird IdP group is listed as a tag passed dynamically in the request". These tags appear under **Experimental → Tag Management** and in **Usage → Tag Usage**. Nothing syncs the other way, and no LiteLLM Teams (the `/team` objects) are created.

This matters if you use LiteLLM Teams. NetBird's integration maps groups to tags, not to LiteLLM teams.

## 3. How budgets work per team

Each layer is independent.

**Layer 1: NetBird policies.** These are enforced before the request reaches LiteLLM ([Limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/policies/limits)).
- A policy connects source groups to providers. Nothing is allowed by default.
- It can cap tokens or USD spend per user and per group, over a fixed window.
- Windows are aligned to the Unix epoch, not sliding.
- The check is `used >= cap` before the request runs. One request can overshoot, and the next one is blocked.
- Account-wide caps are checked first ([Global Limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/global-limits)).
- If a caller belongs to several groups, management picks one matching policy to attribute the request to, preferring uncapped policies and larger remaining budgets ([How it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works)).

**Layer 2: LiteLLM.** The docs say it "applies its own tag and end-user budgets on top, driven by the same NetBird identity."
- Per-group budgets in LiteLLM are **tag budgets** ([LiteLLM tag budgets](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/tag_budgets)).
- You create a tag with the same name as the NetBird group, using `/tag/new` or the UI, with `max_budget`, `budget_duration`, and optionally `rpm_limit` and `tpm_limit`.
- A tag budget that is exceeded returns HTTP 422. Tag rate limits return 429. If any tag on a request is over budget, the request is rejected.
- Per-user budgets use LiteLLM's end-user (customer) budgets, keyed on `x-litellm-end-user-id`, which NetBird sets to the user's email. I did not fetch that page, so check [Customers / End-Users](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/customers).

**Design caveats:**
- **Multiple groups.** A user in several groups sends several tags. If any one tag is over budget, the request is rejected. A user in Engineering and Contractors is therefore bound by both budgets.
- **Tag budgets are not auto-created.** The tag appears dynamically, but it has no budget until you create it in LiteLLM. LiteLLM's baggage-mapping docs say spend is counted from the first request, and that creating the tag with `/tag/new` resets its counter. That statement is written for baggage-mapped tags. I did not verify the same behaviour for body tags, so create budgeted tags before traffic starts.
- **Two sources of truth.** You have to keep NetBird caps and LiteLLM tag budgets consistent yourself. I found no mechanism that syncs them.
- **LiteLLM bug history.** Issue [#27480](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/27480) reported tag budgets silently not enforced when tags came via the `x-litellm-tags` header. It was closed in May 2026. NetBird uses body `metadata.tags`, which that issue says was enforced correctly. Test enforcement on your own LiteLLM version anyway.
- **Mixed windows.** NetBird windows are fixed and aligned to the epoch. LiteLLM's `budget_duration` resets are relative (for example `30d`). The two windows will not line up.

## 4. Are you limited to IdP teams?

Policies are written against NetBird groups, not directly against IdP groups.
- IdP sync is one source of those groups. The [IdP sync docs](https://docs.netbird.io/manage/team/idp-sync) cover Entra (API and SCIM), Okta, Google Workspace, JumpCloud, Keycloak, IIJ ID and generic SCIM. In NetBird Cloud it needs the Team plan or higher. Self-hosted needs an Enterprise licence. The open-source Community Edition does not include it.
- Autonomous agents (no human) get their identity from the peer itself, "the groups assigned to that peer" ([How it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works)). These can be NetBird-native groups.
- The IdP-sync page says synced groups remove the "need for manual grouping". That implies manually managed groups also exist. I did not find an Agent Network page that says you can freely mix manual groups with human users' IdP identities in policies and limits. Treat that as unconfirmed.
- There is an open community discussion about JWT group sync and non-special API groups ([#7288](https://github.com/netbirdio/netbird/discussions/7288)). That suggests the interaction between manually created groups and JWT-synced groups has rough edges. I did not read that thread.

## Confidence and open questions

- **High confidence.** The mechanism: tags in `metadata.tags`, `x-litellm-end-user-id`, the `allow_client_tags` requirement, and the two budget layers. All come from first-party docs.
- **Not verified:**
  - Whether manually created NetBird groups work in Agent Network policies for human users.
  - Whether a NetBird group name that doesn't match any LiteLLM tag is handled safely when you rely on LiteLLM for enforcement.
  - How NetBird's per-user cap and LiteLLM's end-user budget behave together.
  - Agent Network is marked **Beta**, so behaviour may change.

answer:
Compris : you want to know how KServe and vLLM work together. You also want to know how multiple GPUs are handled, and which parallelism is used (tensor, data or pipeline). Finally, you want to know how vLLM options are passed and handled. This is a standard research question, so I'll check the live KServe and vLLM docs.Understood: you asked how KServe and vLLM fit together, how multiple GPUs are handled, which parallelism types are used, and how vLLM options are passed through. I checked the KServe 0.20 docs, the KServe 0.18 release blog and the current vLLM docs.

## 1. How KServe and vLLM fit together

KServe is the Kubernetes control plane. vLLM is the inference engine inside the pod. KServe has two ways to run vLLM.

**Path A: `InferenceService` with the Hugging Face runtime**
- The Hugging Face serving runtime "uses `vLLM` backend engine". If vLLM doesn't support the model, "KServe automatically falls back to the standard Hugging Face backend".
- KServe handles the Kubernetes side: model download, autoscaling, and routing. It also exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints under the `openai/v1/...` prefix, such as `/openai/v1/chat/completions`.
- It picks the CUDA image automatically if the pod requests `nvidia.com/gpu`.
- Source: https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview

**Path B: `LLMInferenceService` (LLMISVC), newer and built on llm-d**
- It is a separate CRD for generative AI. It combines "vLLM's inference engine with Kubernetes orchestration and intelligent routing".
- It adds a Gateway API route, an inference-aware scheduler (KV-cache-aware routing), prefill/decode separation, and multi-node workloads through LeaderWorkerSet.
- The docs say `InferenceService` can serve LLMs "but only for basic single-node deployments".
- Source: https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-overview
- vLLM's own docs list both paths: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/deployment/integrations/kserve/

## 2. Multi-GPU handling and parallelism

KServe delegates parallelism to vLLM and only sizes and schedules the pods. All three types appear, in different places.

| Type | Where it applies | How you configure it |
|---|---|---|
| **Tensor parallelism (TP)** | Splits each layer's weights across GPUs. This is the default for a model too big for one GPU, within a node. | `--tensor-parallel-size` in single-node `InferenceService` and LLMISVC. `workerSpec.tensorParallelSize` in multi-node `InferenceService`. `spec.parallelism.tensor` in LLMISVC. |
| **Pipeline parallelism (PP)** | Splits layers into stages across nodes, for models too big for one node. | `workerSpec.pipelineParallelSize` in `InferenceService`. |
| **Data parallelism (DP)** | Replicates the model so separate batches of requests run in parallel. | `spec.parallelism.data` and `dataLocal` in LLMISVC. Also plain `replicas`. |
| **Expert parallelism (EP)** | Distributes the experts of MoE models (Mixtral, DeepSeek-R1). | `spec.parallelism.expert: true` in LLMISVC. |

**`InferenceService` with the Hugging Face runtime**
- **Single node, several GPUs:** you request N GPUs on the pod and pass `--tensor_parallel_size N` as a runtime argument.
- **Multi-node:** you use the `kserve-huggingfaceserver-multinode` ServingRuntime plus `workerSpec` on the `InferenceService`. KServe docs: "Specifying workerSpec indicates that multi-node functionality will be used."
  - The KServe 0.20 docs say it runs on Ray, with exactly one head pod and workers. KServe 0.18 added an `mp` (multiprocessing) executor as an alternative that needs no Ray head node. The `multinode/executor-backend` annotation switches between `ray` (default) and `mp`.
  - The docs give the mapping `Total GPUs = tensorParallelSize × pipelineParallelSize`. TP is the GPUs per node and PP is the number of nodes.
  - If you ask for TP=16 with 8 GPUs per pod, KServe rewrites it to PP=2 and TP=8.
- **Restrictions in the docs:**
  - Standard deployment mode only.
  - No autoscaling (`autoscalerClass: none`).
  - The model must be on a PVC with ReadWriteMany.
  - NCCL only.
  - `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE` cannot be set via env vars. Use `workerSpec`.
  - The docs warn that changing `pipelineParallelSize` is "not an autoscaling concept".
- Source: https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/multi-node and https://kserve.github.io/website/blog/kserve-0.18-release

**`LLMInferenceService`**
- `spec.parallelism` has `tensor`, `data`, `dataLocal`, `expert` and `dataRPCPort`.
- The multi-node size is `data / dataLocal`, which becomes the LeaderWorkerSet size. For example, `data: 16` and `dataLocal: 8` gives 2 nodes.
- Source: https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-configuration
- A GitHub issue reports that KServe does not create the correct number of pods when `tensor > dataLocal`. I only saw the search snippet, so verify it for your version: https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/4946

**vLLM's own guidance** (https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/serving/parallelism_scaling/):
- If the model fits on one GPU, don't distribute it.
- If it fits on one node, use TP.
- If it needs several nodes, set TP to the GPUs per node and PP to the number of nodes.
- For GPUs without NVLink (the docs name L40S), PP can give better throughput than TP.
- For MoE models, use DP attention with EP or TP for the MoE layers.

**Scaling out for throughput** works differently by path:
- With `InferenceService`, you scale by adding replicas, each a full copy of the model. That is data parallelism in effect, but this is my reading of the docs, not a documented "DP" setting.
- With LLMISVC, you scale through `replicas`, the `data` parallelism setting, or `spec.scaling` with the Workload Variant Autoscaler. That autoscaler can target LeaderWorkerSet in 0.18 and later.

## 3. How vLLM options are handled

**Hugging Face runtime (`InferenceService`)**
- You pass options as container `args` in the ServingRuntime or the `InferenceService`.
- The runtime has its own flags, such as `--model_name`, `--model_id`, `--backend`, `--task`, `--dtype` and `--max_model_len`.
- It also states that "vLLM backend engine arguments can also be specified on the command line and will be parsed by the Hugging Face runtime", and that it "supports **all** vLLM engine arguments".
- Examples listed in the docs: `--tensor_parallel_size`, `--gpu_memory_utilization`, `--quantization`, `--enforce_eager`.
- `VLLM_*` environment variables go in `env`, for example `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE` for CPU deployments.
- The exception is TP and PP in multi-node mode, which must come from `workerSpec`.
- Source: https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview

**LLMISVC**
- There is no wrapper. The pod template is a plain vLLM container (`vllm/vllm-openai`), and you give it `args` directly, such as `--tensor-parallel-size 4` and `--enable-chunked-prefill`.
- You must keep those flags consistent with `spec.parallelism`. I found no documentation saying KServe injects `--tensor-parallel-size` from `spec.parallelism`, so in the docs' own example the same value is written twice.
- Configs can be composed with `baseRefs` to `LLMInferenceServiceConfig`, and any field can be overridden.

## Confidence and open points

- **Confidence:** high for the structure and the parallelism options, because they come from the KServe 0.20 docs and the vLLM docs. Medium for details that changed between 0.16 and 0.20, since the multi-node page describes the Ray-based setup and the 0.18 blog adds the `mp` backend.
- **Open points:**
  - I did not read the controller source. Whether LLMISVC injects `--tensor-parallel-size` itself is therefore unconfirmed.
  - The KServe multi-node page does not say whether pipeline parallelism needs high-speed interconnect between nodes. vLLM's general guidance says tensor parallelism across nodes needs InfiniBand or similar.
  - I did not check the standalone vLLM runtime that GitHub issue #735 mentions as added in v0.20.
- **Which path fits your case:** tell me your model size, GPU count per node and GPU type, and whether you need autoscaling. Then I can say whether `InferenceService` or LLMISVC is the better fit. For example, multi-node `InferenceService` has no autoscaling, while LLMISVC supports it.
